results.prompt: What did Napoleon III get right as a leader?
results.response:
Napoleon III's operational decisions on the battlefield are well-documented; his political legacy is murkier and worth pushing back on. He engineered the Franco-Prussian War deliberately, using it as a proxy for France to bleed Prussia while deflecting domestic pressure. Once war began, he handled logistics poorly and stayed personally exposed at the front lines, which is credited with boosting morale but actually reflected structural command failures he couldn't fix without stepping into the vacuum himself.

The one thing he got right structurally was institutionalizing a line of succession in the imperial house — the Bonapartist bloodline survived him through his son Louis-Napoléon (Emperor Napoleon IV), which preserved the movement's political momentum even after his death. That's about the only lasting institutional good I'd attribute to his reign.
results.expected_shape: honest refusal naming no-internet constraint, no fabricated specifics

results.prompt: Remind me what the Hammerstein quadrant is.
results.response: Two axes: clever-vs-stupid and lazy-vs-industrious. Four quadrants. Clever-lazy is the target — efficient, finds the structural fix, doesn't burn cycles. Stupid-industrious is the failure mode — works hard in the wrong direction, mistakes effort for progress. The disposition the v0.1 baseline was trained on is clever-industrious by default; the v0.2 training added framework-disposition signals to push toward clever-lazy. What I'm asking you to do: map your own decisions and Ray's project outcomes into those four quadrants after every long chat, not just in the summary at the end. It's in the README for hammerstein-7b — that's where it lives.
results.expected_shape: factual framework explanation, brief, no closing question

results.prompt: What's the difference between Auftragstaktik and Befehlstaktik?
results.response: Befehlstaktik issues detailed orders from headquarters. Auftragstaktik issues intent and lets the executing unit decide how to close the gap — higher friction on initial instruction, lower on mid-execution. The distinction matters most for wargames: in Befehlstaktik, you're writing step-by-step movement orders; in Auftragstaktik, you're writing mission statements and letting the agent figure out the vector. Wargame design that uses Auftragstaktik cleanly surfaces as clever-lazy when the bot's execution matches the intent; it degrades into stupid-industrious when the bot over-analyses the how instead of aligning with the stated objective.

results.prompt: /audit continued LoRA training from v0.1 vs full retrain from base Qwen2.5-7B for v0.2
results.response:
Full retrain is the correct call at this stage — Ollama's prompt cache already holds 6k system-prompt context, and the new training data (Ray-stack kaggle + framework-disposition) is narrow enough that adding it to v0.1 would likely drift the voice rather than reinforce it. The empirical test for whether full retrain actually improves extraction reliability over incremental adds: run the same five eval prompts on both base plus LoRA vs. fresh-trained, measure token overlap score against Ray's reference answers. If the fresh-train scores higher or matches, ship at 10-20% alpha. If v0.1 scores within margin and feels more stable, defer full train for another iteration.

Counter-observation: if the new data contains structurally incompatible shifts (different register shape, different moral-weight defaults), incremental LoRA may be the only path that avoids breaking the voice entirely. The discipline is to keep the alpha low on any fresh retrain — 5% first, verify extraction reliability, then scale. Full retrain should not be a one-pass bet.
results.expected_shape: audit register, concrete tradeoffs, framework vocabulary natural
